title: Handling of Waste and Condemned Material and Pest Control

lessons.title: Handling waste and condemned material
lessons.html:
Keeping unfit material out of the food chain

Abattoirs produce large amounts of waste: blood, gut contents (rumen and intestinal contents), manure from lairages, inedible offal, hair, bones, trimmings and wastewater. Some material is condemned during meat inspection because it is unfit for human consumption, for example carcasses or organs affected by disease, abscesses, contamination or parasites. Under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000, condemned material must be controlled so that it can never re-enter the food chain.

Types of material

CategoryExamples
Condemned materialDiseased carcasses or parts, measly meat, abscesses, contaminated parts
Inedible by-productsHair, hooves, horns, some offal not for human use
Process wasteGut contents, manure, blood (if not collected as a by-product), wastewater
General wastePackaging, paper, plastics

Handling condemned material

  • Place it immediately in clearly marked, leak-proof, lockable containers kept only for condemned material. Containers are usually a specific colour and labelled.
  • Keep condemned material separate from edible products at all times.
  • Where required, mark or denature it (for example with an approved dye) so it cannot be passed off as food.
  • Store it in a secure, locked area or remove it promptly to an approved rendering plant, incinerator or disposal site.
  • Keep records of what was condemned, why, the quantity and how it was disposed of.

Hygiene and safety

Condemned material can carry disease. Wear gloves and protective clothing, wash hands after handling, and clean and disinfect containers after emptying. Never take condemned meat home or give it to anyone; it is dangerous and illegal.

Wastewater and solid waste

Wastewater must pass through screens and fat traps and be treated or disposed of according to municipal and environmental requirements, including the National Water Act 36 of 1998. Solid waste such as manure and rumen contents should be removed regularly, as it attracts flies and rodents.

lessons.title: Pest control in the abattoir
lessons.html:
Keeping pests out

Rats, mice, cockroaches, flies, birds and stray animals such as cats and dogs carry bacteria and parasites onto meat and surfaces. A documented pest control programme is a basic requirement for every registered abattoir.

Prevention: keep them out

  • Keep doors closed; use self-closing doors, air curtains or strip curtains.
  • Fit fly screens on windows and ventilation openings.
  • Seal holes, cracks and openings around pipes and cables.
  • Keep the surroundings neat: cut grass, remove rubbish and old equipment where rodents hide.

Remove food and shelter

  • Remove waste and condemned material promptly and keep containers closed.
  • Clean up spills of blood, fat and meat scraps immediately.
  • Keep drains clean and covered with grids.
  • Store supplies off the floor and away from walls so they can be inspected.

Control and monitoring

  • Rodents: tamper-proof bait stations outside the building and traps inside production areas. Poison baits are never used inside production areas where they could contaminate meat.
  • Flies: electric fly killers (insect light traps) placed where dead insects cannot fall onto meat, plus good sanitation.
  • Birds: netting and closing roosting spaces.
  • Crawling insects: inspections and approved treatments by trained operators.

Pest control is usually done by a registered pest control contractor using registered products according to the label (Act 36 of 1947). A site map shows each numbered bait station and trap. Inspections are recorded, including signs of activity and actions taken.

The meat examiner's role

Watch for signs of pests: droppings, gnaw marks, live or dead insects, nests and bird droppings. Report them immediately. If pests or their droppings contact meat, that meat may need to be condemned. Ensure chemicals are never used near exposed meat.

Key points

  • Condemned material goes into marked, lockable containers and never re-enters the food chain.
  • Keep records of condemnations and disposal.
  • Never take condemned meat home.
  • Keep pests out with closed doors, screens and sealed openings; remove food and shelter.
  • Use bait stations outside, traps inside, and record all pest control.
